title: Asynchronous JavaScript: the event loop and callbacks
goal: Predict the order in which synchronous code, timers and callbacks run.

concepts: JavaScript runs one thing at a time (single thread)
The call stack
setTimeout and setInterval hand work to the browser/Node and come back later
The task queue and the event loop
Microtasks (promises) run before the next task (timers)
Callbacks and 'callback hell'

build.task: In day43/: (1) order.js: write 8 snippets mixing console.log, setTimeout(…, 0), setTimeout(…, 100) and Promise.resolve().then(…). Write your predicted output order as a comment before running each, then the actual result. (2) timer.html: a countdown timer page with start, pause and reset buttons and a minutes:seconds display, using setInterval and clearInterval. It must not speed up if you press Start twice. (3) callbacks.js: write loadStep(name, ms, callback) using setTimeout, then chain 3 steps with nested callbacks, and write in a comment why this nesting gets painful.
acceptance: 8 order snippets, each with a prediction written before running and the actual output
Every wrong prediction explained in one line using the words stack, task or microtask
Timer shows mm:ss, pauses, resumes and resets correctly
Pressing Start twice doesn't create a second interval
callbacks.js runs 3 steps in order using nested callbacks

hints: Rule of thumb: all synchronous code first, then all promise callbacks (microtasks), then timer callbacks (tasks), in time order.
Store the interval id: let intervalId = null; on Start, if (intervalId) return; on Pause, clearInterval(intervalId); intervalId = null.

explainBack.q: Take one of your snippets and explain its output order using the call stack, the microtask queue and the task queue.
lookFor: synchronous runs first on the stack
promise .then is a microtask
setTimeout callback is a task
microtasks drain before next task

explainBack.q: Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not run immediately?
lookFor: callback is queued as a task
runs only after the stack is empty (and microtasks done)
0 is a minimum delay, not exact

lastHintExplanation: JavaScript runs synchronous code to completion on the call stack. A setTimeout callback goes to the task queue and a promise .then goes to the microtask queue. When the stack is empty, the event loop runs all microtasks first, then the next task. So the order is sync logs, then .then callbacks, then timers, even with a 0 ms delay.

predict.why: Sync A and D, then microtask C, then timer B.
Sync 3 first, then the 0 ms timer, then the 100 ms timer.

title: Promises
goal: Create and chain promises, and handle errors with catch.

concepts: A promise is a placeholder for a future value: pending, fulfilled, rejected
new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...) to wrap callback code
.then returns a new promise, so you can chain
.catch handles any rejection earlier in the chain; .finally always runs
Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, Promise.any
Always return inside .then when chaining

build.task: In day44/: (1) rewrite yesterday's loadStep as loadStepP(name, ms) returning a promise, and chain 3 steps with .then (flat, no nesting). (2) Write fakeFetch(url) that resolves with fake data after a random 100–600 ms, or rejects 20% of the time with an Error. Use it with .then/.catch/.finally to print a result or a friendly error and always print 'request finished'. (3) Load 4 fake URLs with Promise.all and with Promise.allSettled, and print how the two behave when one fails. (4) Write timeout(promise, ms) using Promise.race that rejects with 'Timed out' if the promise is too slow.
acceptance: 3-step chain with no nested .then
fakeFetch rejects with an Error object, and catch prints its message
.finally prints on both success and failure
Output shows Promise.all failing fast and allSettled reporting every result
timeout() works: a 2000 ms promise with timeout(…, 500) rejects with 'Timed out'

hints: Flat chain: loadStepP('a', 300).then(() => loadStepP('b', 200)).then(() => loadStepP('c', 100)). Returning the next promise keeps the chain waiting.
Random failure: if (Math.random() < 0.2) reject(new Error(`Failed: ${url}`)); else resolve({ url, data: ... }).
timeout: return Promise.race([promise, new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('Timed out')), ms))]).

explainBack.q: What's the difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled? When would you use each?
lookFor: all rejects as soon as one fails
allSettled waits for all and reports status of each
all when you need every result; allSettled when partial results are OK

explainBack.q: Why must you return the next promise inside .then?
lookFor: otherwise the chain doesn't wait for it
next .then runs immediately with undefined
errors aren't caught by the outer catch

lastHintExplanation: Each .then returns a new promise that resolves with whatever the callback returns. If you return another promise, the chain waits for it; if you forget, the next step runs immediately with undefined and its errors escape your .catch. Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects; Promise.allSettled always waits and gives you each result's status.

predict.why: A is skipped; catch handles the error and returns a fulfilled promise, so C runs.

title: async/await and error handling
goal: Write asynchronous code that reads like normal code, with proper error handling and parallel requests.

concepts: async functions always return a promise
await pauses the function (not the whole program) until a promise settles
try/catch/finally with await
Sequential awaits vs parallel with Promise.all
for...of with await for ordered work; why forEach doesn't wait
Top-level await in modules

build.task: In day45/, rewrite all of Day 44 using async/await. Then write: (1) loadSequential(urls) and loadParallel(urls) using fakeFetch, timing both with console.time and explaining the difference in a comment; (2) retry(fn, attempts = 3, delayMs = 300) that retries a failing async function and throws the last error after all attempts; (3) loadWithFallback(url) that returns cached data from a Map if the request fails. Use try/catch/finally properly everywhere.
acceptance: No .then chains in the rewritten code; async/await throughout
Timing output shows parallel is faster than sequential for 4 URLs, with a comment explaining why
retry retries the right number of times, waits between tries and rethrows the last error
loadWithFallback stores successes in a Map and returns cached data on failure
No await inside forEach anywhere

hints: Parallel: const results = await Promise.all(urls.map(u => fakeFetch(u))); starts all requests at once.
retry: for (let i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return await fn(); } catch (e) { lastError = e; await sleep(delayMs); } } throw lastError;
sleep helper: const sleep = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms));
proof: Commit with day45/ files including the timing output in a comment.

explainBack.q: Explain why loadParallel is faster than loadSequential with your timing numbers.
lookFor: sequential waits for each before starting the next
parallel starts all at once
total ≈ slowest vs sum of all
quotes their numbers

explainBack.q: In retry, why do you write return await fn() inside try instead of return fn()?
lookFor: without await, the rejection happens after leaving try
catch wouldn't run
await makes the error throw inside try

lastHintExplanation: Sequential awaits start each request only after the previous one finishes, so the total time is the sum. Promise.all starts them all at once, so the total is roughly the slowest. Inside try, return fn() hands back a pending promise and leaves the try block before it rejects, so catch never runs; return await fn() makes the rejection throw inside the try.

predict.why: async functions always return a promise.

predict.q: async function f() { console.log(1); await null; console.log(2) } f(); console.log(3)
predict.why: f runs synchronously until await, then the rest resumes as a microtask after 3.

goal: Fetch real data from public APIs, handle errors properly, and render it on a page.

concepts: What a REST API is: URLs for resources, HTTP methods for actions
fetch(url) returns a Response; await res.json() for the body
fetch only rejects on network failure: check res.ok for 404/500
Query parameters with URLSearchParams
POST with method, headers and JSON.stringify body
CORS in one sentence: the server decides which websites may read its responses

Show avatar, name, bio, followers and the 5 latest repos with links. Handle: empty input, user not found (404) with a friendly message, network error, and a loading state (disable the button and show 'Loading…'). Also create posts.html that POSTs a new post to JSONPlaceholder (/posts) and shows the returned id.
acceptance: Profile and repos load in parallel with Promise.all
res.ok is checked; a 404 shows 'User not found' (not a crash)
Loading state shown and button disabled during the request
Network errors (try offline mode in DevTools) show a friendly message
All API text rendered with textContent (no innerHTML with API data)
POST to JSONPlaceholder sends JSON with the right header and shows the response id

hints: Helper: async function getJSON(url) { const res = await fetch(url); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`); return res.json(); } Then check the message for 404.
Simulate offline: DevTools → Network → throttling dropdown → Offline.
POST: fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ title, body, userId: 1 }) }).

explainBack.q: Why doesn't fetch reject on a 404? How does your code handle it?
lookFor: fetch only rejects on network failure
404 is a valid HTTP response
check res.ok / res.status and throw

explainBack.q: Explain your loading state: when does it start and how do you make sure it always ends?
lookFor: set before awaiting
cleared in finally
so it ends on success and on error

explainBack.q: What headers and body did you send in the POST and why?
lookFor: Content-Type: application/json tells server the body format
body is a JSON string
method POST creates a resource

lastHintExplanation: fetch resolves whenever the server replies, even with 404 or 500; it only rejects when there's no response at all (offline, DNS failure). So check res.ok and throw yourself. Start the loading state before awaiting and clear it in finally so it ends on both success and error.

predict.why: The request succeeded at network level; the server answered 404, so ok is false.

title: Project: weather app with search, loading and errors
goal: Build a polished weather app on a real API with search, debounced suggestions, and solid loading and error states.

concepts: Reading API docs: endpoints, parameters, response shape
Chaining requests: city name → coordinates → forecast
Debouncing input so you don't send a request on every keystroke
Ignoring out-of-date responses (race conditions) with AbortController
UI states: idle, loading, success, empty, error

resources.title: Open-Meteo: Weather Forecast API docs (no key needed)

build.task: In day47/, build a weather app with Open-Meteo (no API key). Typing a city shows up to 5 suggestions from the geocoding API (debounced 300 ms; cancel the previous request with AbortController). Choosing one fetches the current temperature, a weather description from the weather code, and a 5-day min/max forecast. Show clear loading, empty ('No cities found') and error states. Remember the last 5 searched cities in localStorage as quick buttons. Make it responsive and accessible.
acceptance: Suggestions are debounced (no request per keystroke, check the Network tab)
Older suggestion requests are aborted; fast typing never shows stale results
Current weather and 5-day forecast shown with readable descriptions for weather codes
Distinct loading, empty and error states
Last 5 cities remembered and clickable after reload
Usable with keyboard only and on a phone

hints: Debounce: let t; input.addEventListener('input', () => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(search, 300); }).
Abort: keep let controller; before each search: controller?.abort(); controller = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal }). Ignore errors whose name is 'AbortError'.
proof: Commit with day47/ files. Optional: deploy it to GitHub Pages and link it.

explainBack.q: What problem does debouncing solve, and how does your debounce code work?
lookFor: too many requests per keystroke
clearTimeout resets the timer on each key
request only after pause of 300 ms

explainBack.q: Describe the race condition AbortController prevents.
lookFor: older slower response could arrive after newer one
stale suggestions overwrite fresh ones
abort cancels previous request

lastHintExplanation: Debouncing waits until the user pauses typing: each keystroke clears the previous timer, so only the last one fires. Without aborting, a slow response for 'Pu' could arrive after the response for 'Pune' and overwrite the newer suggestions. AbortController cancels the old request so only the latest one can update the UI.

predict.q: With a 300 ms debounce, a user types 'Pune' with 100 ms between keys and then stops. How many searches run?
predict.why: Each key resets the timer; only the pause after the last key triggers a search.

title: Debug lab: async bugs, and week review
goal: Recognise and fix the four most common async/await mistakes.

concepts: Forgetting await: you get a Promise, not the value
async callbacks in forEach aren't awaited
return without await inside try lets errors escape
Passing resolve() (called) instead of resolve to setTimeout
Unhandled promise rejections and how Node reports them

build.task: Copy the starter into day48/debug/async-bugs.js and run it with node. Expected output: name: Asha; all: [ 'Asha', 'Ravi', 'Meena' ] (in this order every time); safe: Could not load user 99; waited ms ≥ 1000? true. There are 4 bugs. Fix each in its own commit. Then write day48/week8-notes.md with one confident and one weak topic per day for Days 43–47.

starterFiles.name: day48/debug/async-bugs.js

acceptance: Output matches all 4 expected lines; run it 5 times and the order of names never changes
4 separate fix commits naming each bug
No unhandled promise rejection warnings
week8-notes.md covers Days 43–47

hints: 'name: undefined' means user is not what you think. Log user itself.
'all: []' means loadAll returned before any callback finished. forEach ignores the promises its callback returns. Use for...of with await (ordered) or Promise.all with map.
The safe case crashes even though there's a try/catch: the promise rejects after the function has already returned it. And in wait, look closely at what's passed to setTimeout.
proof: Link to your final fix commit.

explainBack.q: Explain each of the 4 bugs in one sentence and your fix.
lookFor: missing await → Promise has no .name
forEach doesn't await → empty array; use for...of or Promise.all
return without await escapes try → return await
resolve() called immediately → pass resolve

explainBack.q: If you fixed loadAll with Promise.all, why is the order still guaranteed?
lookFor: Promise.all keeps results in input order
regardless of which finishes first

lastHintExplanation: 1) fetchUser returns a promise, so without await user.name is undefined. 2) forEach doesn't wait for async callbacks, so names is returned empty; use for...of with await, or Promise.all(ids.map(...)), which keeps input order. 3) return fetchUser(id) leaves the try before the promise rejects; use return await. 4) setTimeout(resolve(), ms) calls resolve immediately; pass resolve itself.
